stances.claim: The pork barrel scam has formally moved from fact-finding into the preliminary investigation phase with the Ombudsman, and readers must understand each step (NBI -> DOJ -> Omb PI -> Sandiganbayan -> SC) to follow the case intelligently.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-explainer architecture (mapping the criminal-justice pipeline as the column's scaffold)

stances.claim: Five different laws govern state-witness immunity and they are not identical -- RA 6981, RA 6770, PD 749, EO 14-A, and the Rules of Court each have distinct standards (most notably whether the witness must 'not appear to be the most guilty'), and the choice of which to invoke shapes who can be discharged.
stances.rhetorical_move: law-inventory technique (cataloging parallel statutes to expose discretionary leverage)

stances.claim: Janet Lim-Napoles should NOT be turned into a state witness at the PI stage; she should be charged alongside the others, with her possible discharge reserved for trial-stage Sandiganbayan approval if absolutely necessary.
stances.rhetorical_move: prudential-prosecution counsel (urging restraint on a contested tactical choice)
stances.confidence: asserted with qualifier ('perhaps, the better way')

stances.claim: Conviction in this case will be difficult, tedious and energy-sapping -- likely beyond President Aquino's term -- because plunder trials are complex (Estrada's alone took 7 years), and only guts, passion, perseverance and public vigilance will move the case to justice.
stances.rhetorical_move: realistic-expectations setting (using historical benchmark to dampen unrealistic timelines)

notable_anecdotes: The Estrada plunder trial took 7 years in the Sandiganbayan -- 'and he was alone' -- used as the durational benchmark for what awaits 38 respondents with 'gilded lawyers,' the most concrete reality check in the column.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban walks readers through the criminal-justice pipeline now activated by the filing of plunder, graft, bribery and malversation complaints before the Ombudsman against 38 persons -- three senators and five former congressmen included. He maps the stages: NBI fact-finding (with whistle-blowers who 'spilled the beans'), DOJ evaluation under Secretary Leila de Lima, preliminary investigation by Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales (who vowed to finish 'in much less than a year'), filing of the information in the Sandiganbayan, trial, and appeal to the Supreme Court. He inventories five distinct laws governing the grant of state-witness immunity -- RA 6981 (WPP, with the 'not the most guilty' standard), RA 6770 (Omb's own authority), PD 749 (no most-guilty requirement), EO 14-A issued by Cory Aquino (unique in applying to civil liability, not just penal/tax), and the Rules of Court (requiring court approval once an information is filed) -- then turns to the strategic question of whether Janet Lim-Napoles should be made a state witness. His answer: prosecute her with the rest; reserve discharge for the trial stage if absolutely needed, noting she is already detained on a separate illegal-detention case in Makati RTC. He closes with the Estrada plunder trial -- seven years in the Sandiganbayan, and Estrada was alone -- as warning that conviction here will be 'difficult, tedious and energy-sapping' and may run beyond President Aquino's term: 'Guts, passion and perseverance are needed... Public vigilance is the price for upholding the rule of law in our democracy.'
